title: Police shootings inquest: Mentally ill woman convinced she was doomed, psychiatrist testifies
subtitle: Sylvia Klibingaitis, later killed by police, had heard Jesus telling her 'she was doomed.'
article: A mentally ill woman shot dead by police believed she was condemned by God to eternal damnation, an inquest heard Tuesday.

Sylvia Klibingaitis, 52, was killed by a Toronto police officer after she left her home with a knife on Oct. 7, 2011. Her death is being examined in a coroner's inquest into the fatal police shootings of three mentally ill people.

A psychiatrist testified Tuesday that Klibingaitis was admitted to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health at her sister's request in October 2009. On her second day in hospital, the deeply religious woman heard a voice, he said.

"She heard absolutely clearly, when she was awake, the voice of Jesus telling her she was condemned, would never have eternal life and would never receive his love," testified Dr. Gerald Sugar, who read the discharge summary.
"That was a recent experience but a very powerful one, which stayed with her all the time I knew her."

Klibingaitis was given a provisional diagnosis of mixed episode bipolar disorder with some psychotic features and was prescribed with an antidepressant, an antipsychotic and a mood stabilizer. After four days in hospital, she showed enough improvement to be able to make decisions for herself, and was discharged seven weeks later with no suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

Sugar met with Klibingaitis on a regular basis for a year after she was discharged from hospital. He testified that at first, she was able to work part-time, make friends and enjoy watching TV and movies.
But Klibingaitis, who had a degree in Christian studies from the University of Toronto and had attended mass all her life, was never able to shake her religious delusions.
She believed "she was doomed," he said. "She could not be saved. God wants to punish her. He wants her to die because she has harmed so many people."

The psychiatrist said he could not find any history of her having harmed people. He testified that he struggled to make sense of her delusions, although there was a traumatic incident in her past that may have contributed to it.

Things worsened when she began to experience a side effect called motor restlessness from one of her medications, which made her shuffle from foot to foot constantly, and she lost her job. In the spring of 2010, Klibingaitis stopped taking some or all of her medication, but she later told the doctor that she resumed taking the pills because she felt a "greater sense of doom."
In early 2011, Sugar asked another psychiatrist for a second opinion, and that doctor took over her care.

The inquest has heard that Klibingaitis visited CAMH on Sept. 27, 2011, and asked to be voluntarily admitted, but changed her mind. Just 10 days later, she called 911, saying that she had a knife and was going to kill her mother. When she left the home still holding the knife, an officer shot and killed her.

Klibingaitis's sister, Lili Steer, questioned the psychiatrist Tuesday about what could have caused her sister's religious obsession. She said she had always wondered what had happened in her sister's past, but never knew.

"She was my best friend from childhood until the day she died," said Steer. "Sometimes she talked about what was going on in her mind. Sometimes she didn't... Now, we are left with her last few words on a 911 call."
